video_title: The NBA's $10 Billion Question: What Happens With the Lakers

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: Mark Walter's multi-league ownership trend in professional sports
quotes.excerpt: Ownership groups that own teams across multiple leagues. You may know about it most recently in Los Angeles.
quotes.quote: Ownership groups that own teams across multiple leagues. You may know about it most recently in Los Angeles, where Mark Walter bought the Los Angeles Lakers just last year. Mark Walter, you may know him as the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers. And if you know him as the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, you're going to be pretty familiar with what he's doing on the side that now owns the Lakers too.

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: Mark Walter's Lakers acquisition and the Dodgers' successful investment model
quotes.excerpt: Mark Walter has bought the Lakers, became the majority shareholder of the Lakers... This idea, most people heard that $10 billion number.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: So, the short version is Mark Walter has bought the Lakers, right? Became the majority shareholder of the Lakers, which also clarify, right, for people who aren't familiar. This idea, I think most people heard that $10 billion number when the Lakers were sold.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Ten billion valuation.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: I was going to say, assume the Lakers sold for $10 billion. That is incorrect, right? It was a valuation of ten, and he already owned, well, was it 27? He was in the 20s already, right?

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: He owned about 27%, him and Todd Boehly, the co-owner of the Chelsea Football Club, owned together and they had a right of first refusal to buy the Lakers. And they they exercised it last year at a $10 billion valuation. I think he bought the team for I mean, like net cash spent, cash, I'm using all air quotes because all these things are not actual cash, but you know, somewhere around like that $5 to $6 billion range. Todd Boehly got in there too. And you know, he already owned the Dodgers, which he bought at a mammoth $2 billion price in 2012 as part of the Guggenheim Group. He owns the Los Angeles Sparks too. And so now he's got this troika of of teams.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: Troika. And it's similar to the Josh Harris, Harris Blitzer Sports playbook in the idea of these wealthy people who see sports teams as a really smart investment vehicle, right? Not for the sports, but they own it because they think that there are these assets that are not maximizing their potential, and therefore if we come in, inject our cash, build them out. Yeah, we want to win, but also we can turn these into juggernauts.

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.summary_phrase: The Dodgers' juggernaut status and how the Lakers might emulate their success
quotes.excerpt: The Dodgers have become this juggernaut... Major League Baseball seems like it's going to be instituting a salary cap.
quotes.quote: We're seeing the Dodgers, right? We're seeing the Dodgers. And I'll kind of give away the ending, we'll go back, right, talking around the story about what the Lakers could look like, right, given everything that Mark Walter is doing. This is, by the way, the NBA's $10 billion question, right? This is what a lot of people around the league are thinking right now is like, what's going to happen to the Lakers now that you have this super billionaire, super successful in sports billionaire that owns the team. Right, and we'll fill in the why it makes a difference. But the so I'm talking to someone from baseball, I said, what's the model, what does this look like? And the person said, well, it's the Dodgers, right? The Lakers look like the Dodgers. That's what it looks like. And the best way to sort of summarize the Dodgers, I think, right, is team going for the baseball's first three-peat in 26 years, I believe, since the late 90s Yankees. And that team and that has become so much a juggernaut that they seem to be Major League Baseball seems like it's going to be instituting a salary cap for the first time in league history, basically just to stop the Dodgers and maybe Steve Cohen too, but that's a separate conversation. So that's that's what the Dodgers have become, right? This juggernaut, it's like a cliché, but that's the word you use for them. And the idea being, can the Lakers be that too?

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.summary_phrase: The Lakers' previous 'cheap' and small front office under Jeanie Buss
quotes.excerpt: Under the previous ownership group, starting with the Bus family... the Lakers were cheap.
quotes.quote: Under the previous ownership group, starting with the Bus family, really even Jerry Buss, but more so under Jeanie, the Lakers were cheap. And I'll use that word even though Jeanie threatened to sue me for using that word to describe her ownership approach. Though it wasn't just flexing a little bit. I am. Well, I, you know, I can write that they lowballed Tyronn Lue and they threatened to sue me, but when ESPN publishes a story outlining the outlining the many ways where they lowballed assistant coaches, I guess that's not defamation. But neither here nor there. But the Lakers had the smallest these are like the facts, right? Whether it's lowballing coaches, tiny analytics department, medical staff, no, I mean, we'll get to no assistant GMs, but not even like no, no executives. Like when I was reporting the book, no, and we'll get to the business side too, but I was reporting the book, I thought one of the great ways that's a great description someone on another team gave me is like when Lakers General Manager, if I needed to reach the Lakers and General Manager Rob Pelinka is on a plane, I don't know who else to call. Like I don't know who the number two is. I don't know who else to call, which is not the case for other teams.

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: Lakers' small, dense organization contrasted with the Dodgers' intricate structure
quotes.excerpt: Rob Pelinka runs basketball ops. Joe and Jesse Buss, two Bus brothers, were the assistant GMs until November.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Rob Pelinka runs basketball ops. Joe and Jesse Buss, two Bus brothers, were the assistant GMs until November when they got unceremoniously thrown out of the organization. And it is a pretty small mom and pop organization beyond that, right? Like they have some smart people there, but there's not a lot of them, which differs, I think. You know, you take the Knicks who are in New York on another coast, you know, they're probably their closest analog. The Knicks have a massive front office. You know, one of the biggest in the league. They pay really well, right? Recognizing that they're in New York, you got to pay to spend and compete there. The Lakers are, you know, completely different. They have, you know, a small scouting department, they have a small analytics department, they have a small strategy department. And they spend on players, but they don't spend everywhere else. And I think that's the interesting part. As you said, if the Dodgers are the model for what the Lakers are doing, the Dodgers are known probably to me, I think, the most intricately run, most interesting sports organization, right? Like, yes, the success is there. But what they do as an organization to me is really fascinating. They're immensely successful. They have a top-down model from the MLB side all the way down through their minor leagues. I covered baseball for a bit. They hired Andrew Friedman, who was the president of the Tampa Bay Rays for a number of years, took them to a lot of success that a team like in that market shouldn't be able to do. And what he's left there has withstood the test of time too. And they plucked him from Tampa Bay, made him their president and hired a bunch of really smart executives beyond that. I think really were successful in player development, right? Their analytics, all that type of all the stuff that you need to do in baseball. And now Andrew Friedman, sorry to cut you off, him and Farhan Zaidi, who was a disciple of Billy Beane and the Oakland A's and was the GM of the San Francisco Giants, I think he worked in LA too for a period of time, are now kind of overseeing the Dodgers-ification of the Lakers too.

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.summary_phrase: Lakers' previous spending was a choice; new ownership is 'McKinsey-fying' the organization
quotes.excerpt: Jeanie Buss's decision to not do the things, that was made by choice... Mark Walter wants to put this money in the team.
quotes.quote: I also do want to hit because you asked me a question at the beginning and we went down this path, but the idea of like, can can this baseball approach work in the NBA, right? And I think that's you and I we talked offline about this how there are people around the NBA who sort of have this I'll call it this hater version, like, yeah, but baseball's different than basketball, right? You know, baseball's built for analytics and it's a static game. And I mean, I think you you could probably be a good GM without watching a baseball game if you just give you if you just use all the numbers, you could probably build a good team if you know what you're doing. Exactly, right? Exactly. That's exactly that. Basketball is very much not that, which is one of the my favorite things about the sport. And I talked to other I've you've talked to people about this, I have too, and I do think that people who are saying like, the NBA has always trailed other sports and specifically baseball and its approach to critical thinking, right? In many ways. That's sort of what Daryl Morey, why he was able to become famous because he found these voids that he was able to fill. Sam Presti too. And I think people who think that like the Dodgers people's the skill of these Dodgers executives is the ability to identify which metrics should be used for player valuation is missing the point of what those guys are good with, right? So Andrew Friedman is not going to come in and say, you know what we should be looking at, uh, three-point percentage, you know, teams that shoot threes win finals, and that's what we need to do. It's not that, right? That's not that's not the skill set. And that's not me making making this up reporting this story, talking to people. I talked to Alex Anthopoulos, who's the GM of the Atlanta Braves. Really interesting, basically, he left the Blue Jays after winning executive of the year, couldn't come to a contract, and instead of going to another team, chose to respect that Andrew Friedman, these guys have, basically decided to go to the Dodgers as an assistant GM, I don't remember his official title is, right? But as an assistant GM to I think he might have used the phrase grad school for to me, like when I was talking to him, just to basically go to uh, not baseball grad school, right? Not that, but executive and front office grad school. And that's a distinction. And he said it made him a better GM since after he left. And I remember asking him, like, or I asked him, what are some examples? Like, give me some specific you can give. And I think the quote was along the lines of like, these weren't two wise men sitting there, the two wise men being Andrew Friedman and Farhan Zaidi, saying, you know what the key to winning baseball games is, uh, strong pitching staff, right? Like that wasn't that. It was about how to build out build out an organization, how to critically analyze data, and how to ask the right questions and all that kind of stuff. And I think anyone who thinks that's what the Dodgers guy is going to bring to the Lakers organization, right? So the point if they decide that, you know what, having looked across the NBA, we real we realize that where you need to be really good is strategy and cap management and finding the loopholes, then they're going to find that, and then they're going to go out and get the guys who are best at that, right? That's what they're going to do. And I think that's going to be the difference here.

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: Transferability of skills and Lakers' hiring challenges
quotes.excerpt: What's really worked in baseball may not really work in basketball... Can you find those ways to win the margins in the NBA?

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: What's really worked in baseball may not really work in basketball, right? I know that's an obvious thing to say, but these are two different sports. And I'm curious how they go about doing this and and how into the weeds they get. You know, if you look at what they just did recently, they hired one assistant GM from the New Orleans Pelicans. They hired literally someone who was working for an aerospace company, right? They they hired I think it was called that, right? The company was called like aerospace company or something. That's the name that like sounded like something from a Looney Tunes villain or whatever. I saw that. Yeah, they hired Rohan Ramadas, who is their new assistant GM of like, I think some combination of cap and analytics and strategy and all these types of things. And so they still have one more assistant GM hired to make who runs scouting. And I'm curious what they do. As you said, like, you know, I think they've struck out on a number of candidates. You reported Steve Senior, Minnesota Timberwolves assistant GM had turned them down. I'd heard that before they hired Ramadas that someone else had turned them down for that position too.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: Yeah, they're being rejected everywhere. Or if they're not being turned down outright, the people are turning down the maybe not offers, but the inquiries, right? And kind of being like, ah, no, not for me.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Yeah, and and, you know, I think part of that is questions about how long Rob Pelinka might stay in the job. Obviously, new ownership group, new decisions, decision-makers, maybe they'll want. Although with the Dodgers, you know, Ned Colletti, who was the GM there, he stayed for a number of years. They didn't just come in and clean house. So we'll see what they do on the Lakers side. But it, you know, regardless of that, like, to your point, the Lakers have been a small organization in that the power was very densely accumulated, right? It was Jeanie Buss, it was Linda Rambis, it was Kurt Rambis, the former, you know, long-time assistant coach and and Lakers player from the 1980s, and Rob Pelinka were kind of the brain trust there. That's it, right? And that was it. And they had some smart, you know, like I said, Nick Mazzella has been seen as kind of like a key of their scouting operation, right? Running the South Bay Lakers. Lakers G-League team, by the way, going to be in Coachella next year, which is awesome. I really hope they make everyone dress for those games like they're going to actual Coachella. And maybe they make the players dress like they're going for actual Coachella. That'd be fun.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: But is that again, I know you're on I find that so telling that that's a it sounds funny, moving the G-League team is a big move, but that's a big move that they made pretty quickly under the new team business operation president Lon Rosen, right? Like we're no, this is dumb. We're leaving money on the table with this with this G-League team in our facility. Uh, let's move them. Let's get them out of here and let's make some more money. And that's like that happened pretty quickly and without people, uh, I kind of surprising people around the league, I believe.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Yeah, and and I mean, I think they're going to work with Irving Azoff, uh, the former Eagles manager, who runs the property in Coachella. They brought in a number of Dodgers people on the business side too. So this is this is all across the organization. And I guess the question to me is, what will be left of the old Lakers? And does it matter if anything remains?

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.summary_phrase: Lakers' organizational upheaval and key decisions
quotes.excerpt: I think the answer to your question is not much... The Rambises, there was reported, I believe Baxter Holmes at ESPN reported, right, that they got some sort of balloon payment connected to the sale of the team.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: I think the answer to your question is not much, right? I really think we're on the uh, you know, kind of seeing the the Rambises, there was reported, I believe Baxter Holmes at ESPN reported, right, that they got some sort of balloon payment connected to the sale of the team. I hope I have that information right. I think I'm fairly certain I do that they were

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Good for you, just throwing stuff out and then throwing stuff out before you verified it. Now you're going to go backcheck and Google it while we're talking on the podcast so you can see.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: I'm actually not I'm just going to let it ride. But they anyway, then Rob Pelinka got an extension before the sale went through, which many people think was sort of making sure Jeanie making sure her guy was taken care of before the sale comes through. Like I if you look at the old Lakers, it's it's Rob Pelinka, it's the Rambis, as I like to call them, and it's Jeanie, who's officially somehow held onto that governor title despite owning only 20% of the team. Kudos to her, the one owner who figured out actually had to pull that off without losing that, you know, six months later and without the yeah, remember that that agreement we had that I'd still be governor, we're going back on that.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Cuban and and Celtics Grossbeck style, right? That that's why you got it on paper. Grossbeck didn't have the 15% necessary to be governor. Bill Chism only I would guess Bill Chism probably has as much of a share of the team as Jeanie Buss does and the Bus family. She remains the governor. Yeah, for I think five years, right? Is how long that term is before I I would assume at some point Mark Walter does want to take over.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: Correct.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: But and I assume that, you know, the question is how while Jeanie's in charge, does that mean that Rob will be in charge? Does that mean that Kurt Rambis will be, uh, have some say? Does that mean that Linda Rambis will have some say? Like all those are very important characters. And it's almost in conflict, right? That way of doing things and having those people in charge, uh, is in conflict with building a larger organization, right? Like, you know, the people that Rob Pelinka listens to, and I think they're smart people in the you know, the Lakers organization, right? Like Phil Chang does analytics for them, Marshall Raider does strategy for them, Nick Mazzella said scouting for them. But you're going to add more people it seems like, and that's not going to stop. And if you add more people and you build out this organization and and you hire one assistant GM, another assistant GM is coming, who does Rob Pelinka listen to? Right? Who does he trust? Who does he listen to? Trust is different. Listen is listen is separate, right? Who does he trust?

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: I mean, now we're getting into we, you know, Rob Pelinka is a master survivor, right? So I kind of joke that you're going to he's going to start sounding like a Sloan Sports conference panel now, every press conference he does, because he thinks or works in some like baseball, uh, some baseball lingo, like, oh, I thought this signing was a home run, just like Shohei Ohtani hit last night. You know, he kind of knows how to survive. The question is, how much longer does he want to do it also, right? If he's sort of got this, uh, I want to call it a balloon payment, you can call it a golden parachute, right? Whenever this last contract extension was. This offseason, I think, I know not to be too X and O's, but this offseason is going to be huge for him and them in terms of like, can he prove that he can build a team around Luka? And if it doesn't go well, he's probably in trouble. And if it goes well, he can maybe hang around. But I do think the Lakers old ways, like they're we're on the last legs here of the, you know, I know it's we're talking about a group of foursome, two of which are women, but it's still like the version of a bunch of old men sitting in a cigar room making deals, right? That's what the Lakers what the Lakers ownership and management structure was, uh, and that seems that's going to be long gone.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: And it does come at an interesting time, right? Now, they have Luka Doncic. They've reoriented the franchise around Luka. Austin Reaves can be a free agent this summer. LeBron James will be a free agent this summer. They have some very important roster decisions to make. And this comes at a time where it's just large organizational upheaval. And so it's two things all in one. And and that's why I ask like, who gets listened to, who has the juice, so to speak, right? Like, when important decisions get made, you got to know where the information is coming from. You got to know who to listen to, who to trust. And so all this is kind of happening at a as an all at once type of situation in LA.

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.excerpt: Smart sports executives, those are skills that could be applied across the spectrum.
quotes.quote: I wouldn't bet against them. I kind of I've landed in the place here where I feel like smart sports executives, those are skills that could be applied across the spectrum. And yeah, maybe you can be maybe you end up like Paul DePodesta with the Browns, right? And that went famously wrong, famously bad. I don't know. Friedman, I'm not a baseball reporter. I've done some reporting on this. He seems to have a different sort of reputation. And talk about the soft skills and the EQ and the ability to hang and he's a former college baseball player, which sounds dumb, but that makes a difference. This isn't just like some he's not your cliché. He's not Jonah Hill from Moneyball, right? I just think this stuff makes a difference. I wouldn't bet against him. I really wouldn't.

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: Josh Harris's multi-team ownership and leadership style
quotes.excerpt: The language they speak is different than the language that's spoken of traditional basketball guys.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: Daryl Morey is out of a job now. Maybe he'll be around in Los Angeles a little bit from time to time next season and beyond. You know, like, I would be curious to see if that's what they do. You know, they wouldn't be the first to take in a fired GM and bring him in as a whatever and be around the team and and try to get that. And he speaks their language a lot, I think. And you know, that that's kind of like, I think the interesting part here too is you see a lot of owners come into the NBA now, certainly in baseball, but even in the NBA now, and the language they speak is different than the language that's spoken of traditional basketball guys, right? And so we've seen a lot more strategy type folks get hired as GMs. Not a lot of analytics folks, I think, but still, you know, some or at least the importance of analytics and strategy. And so the language of the the ownership speaks has to be the language that the front office speaks and especially the head of the front office. GM, who has the manager, executive vice president, all the BS titles that I'm honestly sick and tired of. And this will be Sam Presti's legacy. And I hate him for it. All these fake titles. I blame him. And uh, and uh, yeah, I mean, that's that's, you know, that's an advantage that those guys have. And, you know, that like you're talking about Rob Pelinka having to figure that out, like that's the language he's going to have to speak, right? He's going to have to speak about cap strategy, uh, five years down the line and about the, you know, the loopholes that you can exploit and about the the penumbras that you can take advantage of and find, right? And so I'm curious to see how that comes along. Because for so long, you know, like the the skill of running the Lakers was being able to draw in Los Angeles. It was being able to draw in the big market. It was about saying, hey, come play in LA and be awesome and be super famous and take advantage of living in LA. And it worked. Like it was a great strategy. It sounds simple, but it was so efficient that it didn't need to be anything more than that. But now you need more than that. You know, right? Like you talk about the Knicks, the how the Knicks have gotten to the NBA Finals is not been, hey, come and live in New York and play in New York and take advantage of all that. That famously failed from them for them for so long. And like they just made a really just one really astute move after another with a really smart front office, a non-traditional front office, so to speak, and like just layered one really good move after another, had a really smart cap strategy guy in Brock Aller who helped them, you know, got some wins in the draft with Walt Perrin, who ran as AGM running the scouting for them, right? And they made it all work together. And now they're in the finals because they put a little bit of the old juice, which is a little bit of nepotism with Jalen Brunson and finding the right guy who turned into an amazing and amazing player. And uh, you know, like trading for Josh Hart, turning stuff into Cat, uh, you know, like turning two guys who were drafted and homegrown into OG Anunoby like all that just meshed and the alchemy, the secret sauce that you need to make a team work, it just worked there. And so I'm curious with the Lakers who go forward. I guess one thing is, look, if you look at Philly, your first book was tanking to the top about the process era Sixers, which um, that team is now that version of that team is now I think officially thrown into the dustbin of history. Like Daryl Morey was an outgrowth of I'm not I mean, I'm saying that facetiously, but also like this is a pivot, right? Like Sam Hinkie, Bryan Colangelo, um, Elton Brand, Daryl Morey, who was, you know, former colleagues with Sam Hinkie like that, that I think we've we see the clear break here. Whoever comes next, we don't know. But Josh Harris has owned him and David Blitzer have owned the Sixers for 15, 16 years now. He's since bought the Commanders. They own a soccer team. There's the New Jersey Devils. There's an EPL team. Like this is almost like the prototype version of Mark Walter has building in LA. Is there something to be learned from what they've done with the Sixers or something to avoid from what they've done with the Sixers?

quotes.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
quotes.summary_phrase: 76ers' business success vs. on-court struggles and Josh Harris's leadership

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: They are a great example of they've nailed it from a business perspective, right? You might I always forget, I shouldn't know. Well, they bought the Sixers for was it $450 million was the valuation? I think it was like $300 million. I get them and the Warriors, like they're basically in consecutive years, I believe, around the same time, sold for that. I don't know. Well, the Sixers go for now, four, three, I don't know, whatever. Oh, no, way more than that. They would they would probably crack $6 billion, I would guess. And this wasn't an accident, right? Like they've talked about this, but they basically they applied the private equity playbook to their purchase of the Sixers and other sports teams. The idea of we're going to buy a distressed asset that we think can be torn down and then built back up. And people used to think the idea was to flip it. I'm not convinced that that wasn't the plan originally and that they just decided, you know what, we like being sports owners, right? Like this is fun to own the team and it gets us in rooms and things like that. And it's cool. And now people know Josh Harris as opposed before he was known as the guy who just made like an all-time great chemical company bet. I'll bet I assume the name, some kind of like it's known as like the greatest like private equity move, transaction, I don't know what you want to call it, ever. They've they've nailed the business side, right? They got in before that media deal, before sort of the first giant media deal that kicked off these content, you know, streaming wars and all that stuff. Before the NBA took off, all these things, they nailed it. On the court, they've had trouble. Let's say the Sixers specifically. We'll see the Commanders. The Sixers specifically, there's been, you know, they have issues choosing a leader to sort of give the reins to, hand the reins to and allowing that person to operate. And I think the biggest mistake or the biggest weakness among for Josh Harris, and this was said to be recently by somebody talking about the Daryl Morey firing is he he reacts strongly to public pressure, public and he's looks for someone to blame when that public pressure comes down, right? And you've seen that throughout his history, whether Sam Hinkie made many mistakes, why Sam Hinkie gone? Why was he fired or replaced, whatever word you want to use, because public pressure was growing, the process wasn't working, things looked bad. I needed to blame someone, it's his fault. Let me go down and down and down the line, right? And why did he fire Daryl Morey? Or, excuse me, parted ways mutually with Daryl Morey, right? I mean, lots of reasons, but I'm the Knicks fan takeover of of uh Philadelphia in that game four, 100% contributed to that. When he's sitting there and he's saying, this sucks, somebody needs to go for this, right? And that's, you know, it's strange to be an owner for so long and so many teams and not realize that such an approach doesn't work. And I guess that would be the thing that Mark Walter, he hasn't done that, not that he's had reason to. The Dodgers are amazing, right? So I guess there's no there's no public. I mean, they've made it to five World Series, they won three of the last like five or six or so. And it took them a while to get there. Right. Early on, he could have done like the uh I'll say a George Steinbrenner like thing, like, you know, Ricky Bobby, we ain't first, we're last, let's fire somebody, right? After um when when there was that little drought before they won the 2020 or 20, whatever that COVID 2021 World Series was. So yeah, uh, so that's a weird part. The other weird part about the I mean, we're on a tangent now. I don't know if you have any thoughts on this, but just buying the Commanders, what they go, $6 billion valuation, whatever that was. $6.05 billion. Right. That was that was going to the opposite playbook of like the buying low on a team, um, which was interesting too. I don't know if that was a result of them doing their internal analysis and thinking that there's still growth. And if, you know, that asset will grow or just like, no, man, the NBA is the minor leagues and like, I just want to be an NFL owner. Like that's the that's the room to be in. So I don't know about that. That I find that interesting.

quotes.excerpt: Josh Harris has had the opposite problem where... he reacts strongly to public pressure.

text_blocks.speaker: Yaron Weitzman
text_blocks.text: Josh Harris has had the opposite problem where, I mean, you see you were naming the different Sixers executives, lead executives, you left off one when Brett Brown was the interim after Bryan Colangelo was fired, whatever, you know, uh, burner gate. I bring that up because while that was happening, not only was Brett Brown then the head coach and also random minority owner David Heller was also acting like the GM, right? And that's like, like that's a weird situation. You talk about different guys having access to the owner and your ear. And then we have Elton Brand takes over, and there's four other people in the front office who believe they're actually in charge and are emailing Josh Harris their thoughts on things, and there you have a muddled leadership structure, and that creates a Game of Thrones situation and just all sorts of issues. And Mark Walter seems to have figured out, in conjunction with Andrew Friedman, because I think that goes hand in hand, has sort of figured out, seemingly figured out a way to not fall prey to that. I mean, the Dodgers, we talked about Anthopoulos, they're like, their front office has had like five people in there who could all be all qualified to be a number one guy, right? And all in an NBA world, I could see it where I think it's a little more cutthroat in the NBA executive world. I could see there some being some backstabbing and trying to get ownership's ear and sort of some obviously, you repeat the phrase, some Game of Thrones type stuff going on. And that has not been the case in Dodgerland.

quotes.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
quotes.summary_phrase: WNBA Sparks' analytics focus and Lakers' potential strategy
quotes.excerpt: With the Sparks at least, Walter has owned them for a while, it seems like now this past offseason was where they kind of started leveling up.

text_blocks.speaker: Mike Vorkunov
text_blocks.text: With the Sparks at least, Walter has owned them for a while, it seems like now this past offseason was where they kind of started leveling up. You know, their hires were they hired an assistant GM from the NBA, and they hired kind of like an analytics team. And so that was a big point of emphasis for them. So I'm curious to see if that happens on the Lakers too, where the big point of emphasis for them is analytics and what strides they can make there. Maybe it's a little bit different because, you know, in W the W obviously so far behind in analytics and infrastructure than, you know, the NBA is, no matter what team. And how much of an emphasis they put on that, but, you know, that's that's one kind of maybe maybe that's one sign of how this all goes. And so I guess after all that, after nearly 36 minutes of talking and gibber-jabbering and pontificating, we've landed with, we'll see how it goes.
